Development guide

Agentic coding maturity

How far to let an agent go, level by level. The ladder runs from writing every line yourself (L0) to a dark factory where you only step in by exception (L5). At every level the question is the same: what does a person still read, and when?

Draft research reference. Based on published research and practitioner accounts, not local deployment tests.

For the practices behind each level, read How the concepts fit together in Concepts.

Key points

  • Autonomy is a setting chosen per task and per deployment, not a property of a team or a tool. "Maturity" is the capability to choose and support a higher setting safely.
  • This page synthesises L0–L5 from several frameworks; its role labels and verification guidance are not a one-to-one mapping.
  • Score per task and cap by risk; L5 is a direction, not a target — unattended autonomy suits exploration and throwaway work, not production defaults.

Where are we?

The five-levels framing[1] describes delegation distance: how much of the work an agent does before a person has to understand it. The Knight First Amendment Institute[4] describes human roles from operator to observer. This page adapts those labels; they do not map one-to-one to Shapiro’s levels or define approval authority. Addy Osmani's agentic autonomy levels[2] push the framing further: autonomy is a property of a deployment for a task, not of a person or a tool, and capability is something you grow deliberately through feedback loops. The AI Codebase Maturity Model[3] reaches a similar conclusion from a different direction: progress comes from tightening feedback loops, not from chasing a level.

So this page separates two things that maturity models often blur. The level is the autonomy setting for one task. Maturity is the team's capability to choose a higher setting for that task — and to support it — without losing the ability to detect and undo mistakes. A team can run L3 on one workflow and L1 on another — Qodo's L1–L4 earned-autonomy framework, analysed by Futurum, scopes autonomy per workflow in the same way[12].

Self-test. Pick the last three changes your team shipped. For each one, answer: what did a person read, and when? Every line? Every diff? Evidence of checks? Nothing until after release? The answers describe oversight for each task, not the team as a whole. Also examine the permissions, evidence and applicable approval policy before deciding what level of delegation is appropriate.

Fictional example. Maya’s small-business asset-management app needs a handover-form wording change. For this L2 illustration, a developer permits the agent to edit only the form and its tests, not deploy or change permissions. The developer compares the wording with the agreed text, runs relevant checks, reads the diff and retains the results. For a reporting change, the team instead first agrees what totals must be correct, restricts the agent to a test environment and independently checks representative totals. The authorised decision maker decides whether to merge and release each change; neither outcome is assumed.

The ladder L0 to L5

The levels follow Dan Shapiro's five levels framing[1], which already includes L0, and the role names adapt the Knight First Amendment Institute[4]. Addy Osmani's levels[2] describe a different six-level model — Assist, Supervised action, Scoped task delegation, Goal-driven autonomy, Parallel delegation, and Managed-by-exception orchestration — and argue that a single ladder cannot capture both how far one agent goes and how well many agents are coordinated. The level descriptions and role labels are this page’s synthesis, not one-to-one claims about either source. Numbers are not comparable across frameworks. The reading patterns are illustrations, not approval, merge or release policy; apply the authority for the actual change.

Summary of the six levels: agent scope, what the person still reads, and a consideration for further delegation.
LevelName (role)Agent scopePerson still readsFurther delegation
L0BaselineNo delegation; autocomplete at mostEvery line, as the authorTry delegating a bounded chore to an agent on request
L1OperatorAgent helps on request inside granted toolsEvery line of small tasksConsider delegation across files with suitable test feedback
L2CollaboratorAgent edits code, runs tests, reworks within limitsEvery diff before it shipsDelegate a broader task with credible independent evidence; parallel work is optional
L3ConsultantOne or more agents work under supervision; parallel work is optionalTask evidence; code inspection may still be neededBroader goal delegation with risk-appropriate evidence and human decisions
L4ApproverAgent plans and executes a broader goal within limits; triggers and persistence are optionalGoals, plans, exceptions, final evidenceOnly consider an authorised unattended route with independent evidence, monitoring and tested recovery
L5ObserverAuthorised automation can release without a readerOutcomes, by exceptionNo next level on this page — see the direction-not-target section

These optional component roles are examples, not proof of a level or required purchases. Gateways, memory, sandboxes and skill packs do not guarantee safety: assess data access, identity, network and host controls for the deployment.

L0 — Baseline: you write every line

L0 is the no-agent baseline, included so the ladder has a floor. You write the code; an autocomplete suggestion is the most delegation. For example, try delegating a bounded chore to an agent on request, if appropriate. Concepts that apply here: context engineering (what you paste into the prompt) and verification engineering (how you check your own work).

Possible supporting components — An optional coding client can offer suggestions; use verification to check the authored change.

L1 — Operator: the agent helps when asked

This page calls the L1 role operator: the person prompts, reviews, and remains accountable for every line. Shapiro’s L1 describes delegating discrete tasks; his L0 already includes autocomplete. The Concepts that make this level useful rather than busywork: context engineering and harness engineering — Osmani sets the ceiling for the level by risk and reversibility[2].

Possible supporting components — Models generate suggestions, a coding client presents them, and a harness can bound tool use; the person checks the result.

L2 — Collaborator: the agent does the typing, you read the diffs

At L2 the agent edits files, runs tests and reworks within agreed limits, and the person reviews every diff before it ships. This page calls the role collaborator. This is where loop engineering and verification engineering start to carry weight: the agent's rework loop is only as good as the checks it runs. The coding agents page covers which tools sit here; the harness page covers what keeps the loop bounded.

Possible supporting components — A harness can constrain the agent; verification checks the change and a sandbox can limit execution exposure.

L3 — Consultant: supervise delegated work and review evidence

At L3 this page illustrates a person supervising one or more agents and reviewing evidence; inspecting a diff may still be necessary. Parallel agents and worktrees are optional, not a level criterion. Shapiro’s L3 specifically describes reviewing many diffs[1]; this page uses a different boundary. Gametime describes its own repository-level assessment[13], not a per-task classification.

Possible supporting components — An agentic development environment can coordinate work and verification supplies evidence. If parallel work is useful, worktrees separate working copies; they are not a security boundary.

L4 — Approver: delegate a broader goal

At L4 the agent can plan and carry out a broader goal within agreed limits. A persistent agent or event trigger is optional, not a defining feature. People set goals and authorised roles make applicable approval, merge and release decisions. The workflows and factories and verification pages discuss orchestration and evidence.

Possible supporting components — If useful, persistent agents can continue work, context and memory can supply retained information, and a harness can bound actions. Authorised people retain applicable approval decisions.

L5 — Observer: outcomes by exception

At L5 an authorised automation route can carry a change to release without a person reading it first; the person watches outcomes and intervenes by exception. This page calls the role observer. Shapiro's March 2026 dark factories post describes StrongDM's Attractor — a feedback-loop factory explained by StrongDM's CTO Justin Massa — alongside Trycycle, Shapiro's own minimal skill[9]; the StrongDM account is a vendor self-description, not an independently verified benchmark. The Oversight Ladder[10] is explicit that this level suits "exploration and throwaway work, not production a business depends on". Concepts behind it: the software factory with light and dark routes, guardrails, and model selection.

Possible supporting components — A software factory may coordinate an authorised policy route; verification supplies independent evidence. Monitoring, a stop mechanism and realistic recovery remain necessary.

Verification is the gate

This page recommends stronger evidence as delegation increases; it does not prescribe a universal gate or attribute fixed thresholds to the verification concept. A credible independent oracle is an expected result or assessment grounded outside the agent’s own output. Protect the checks, inputs and retained evidence from the authoring agent; protecting a weak check alone does not make it credible. Choose tests, independent review and recovery for the task’s risks. The verification scan discusses methods. These checks have limits and do not guarantee safety.

Illustrative checks to consider at each level, adjusted to the task’s risk.
Climb toPossible checksWhy
L1You can run the code and read what the agent suggestsIncorrect suggestions can become shipped defects; review and test for the risk
L2Automated tests exist and the agent runs them in its loopThe agent now types; the person reads diffs, checks can help catch defects that review misses
L3Independent expected results and protected checks and evidenceA weak or self-approved check can miss a defect even with one agent
L4Independent evidence and risk-appropriate recoveryBroader delegated work needs credible evidence and a way to recover
L5Authorised route, monitored exceptions, proven stop and rollbackAn authorised release route needs independent evidence and intervention capability

Addy Osmani frames the same gate as three questions to answer before raising autonomy on a task[2]:

  • How quickly will we know we're wrong about what it's doing? Detection latency sets the ceiling on how much damage an autonomous run can do.
  • How cleanly can we undo what it's doing? Compare the realistic recovery time and irreversible effects with the task’s risk; rollback alone may not undo all harm.
  • What would prove we're right about what it's doing? The check must be independent of the agent that produced the work.

The two plateaus

Both organisational and technical constraints can limit further delegation. Naming them helps teams diagnose a stall instead of blaming the tool.

L2 to L3: reviewer fatigue

At L2 the person reads every diff. Parallel work can increase review volume, but is not needed for L3. Skimming is not a substitute for credible independent evidence. Anthropic’s measurement work[8] reports longer unattended Claude Code sessions while many sampled tool calls still involved people; it does not establish a safe review threshold.

L3 to L4: spec quality and supervision

Broader goals require clear scope, expected results and supervision. Steve Yegge’s account, analysed by Augment Code[11], describes coordination challenges when agents outnumber supervisors. Triggers and persistent agents are optional; human review or approval of a change can remain necessary at any level. Shapiro’s Trycycle account[9] describes a plan–implement–check loop.

Gametime's published levels show the same pattern at repository scale: web and mobile repos at L3, the backend at high L2 on Shapiro's framework[13]. Score per task and per repo, cap by risk, and let different parts of the system sit at different levels.

Score per task, cap by risk

A team does not have a level; a task does. The Futurum analysis of Qodo's L1–L4 earned-autonomy framework says the same in Qodo's numbering: "a team can operate at L4 for some workflows while keeping others at L3"[12]. The METR study[6] of 16 experienced open-source developers on 246 tasks in familiar repositories using early-2025 AI tools adds a setting-specific warning about measurement: developers' own estimates of how much the agent sped them up were far more optimistic than observed completion times — so score tasks on observable behaviours (what the person read, which checks ran, whether rollback was needed), not on self-reported velocity.

Before raising autonomy on a task, write the run contract. Osmani's checklist[2] covers:

  • Goal — the outcome, in one sentence.
  • Scope — which files, services and systems the agent may touch.
  • Non-goals — what the agent must not do, even if it sees a way.
  • Tools and permissions — exactly what the agent can run and change.
  • Stopping condition — when the agent must stop and ask.
  • Evidence — what the agent must produce to prove the work.
  • Escalation — who decides when the agent is unsure.
  • Budget — time, tokens and cost ceiling for the run.

Then cap by risk. Osmani's metrics for judging whether autonomy is working[2]: mean time between interventions, longest successful unattended run with accepted work, defect escape rate, and token cost per accepted change. If interventions cluster, the level is too high for that task; step down.

What the delivery system needs to support

The organisational axis matters as much as the task axis. The 2025 DORA report[5], based on roughly 5,000 professionals, reported an association between AI adoption and worse delivery stability, and described how surrounding practices influence outcomes — "AI doesn't fix a team; it amplifies what's already there". DORA names seven capabilities that magnify AI's benefits: a clear and communicated AI stance, healthy data ecosystems, AI-accessible internal data, user-centric focus, strong version control, small batches and quality internal platforms[5]. The transformation page covers building those capabilities; the short version for this ladder is that your delivery system caps the level any task can safely reach. Weak version control or slow feedback can limit the autonomy appropriate to a particular task; DORA’s association does not establish a universal L3 ceiling. The delivery scan covers the release and rollback side of that cap.

L5: a direction, not a target

L5 is the level most easily misread as a destination. Three cautions:

  • Vendor self-description. The best-known L5 account is StrongDM's Attractor factory, explained by its CTO in Shapiro's March 2026 dark factories post[9]. That is one company's account of its own system — useful as a pattern, not as evidence that L5 is proven at scale.
  • Unattended autonomy has a domain. The Oversight Ladder[10] is explicit: Level 5 is for "exploration and throwaway work, not production a business depends on", and "treating Level 5 as the goal is how expensive mistakes reach production".
  • No proven general playbook. There is no public, independently verified playbook for climbing from L4 to L5. The Yegge analysis[11] describes the coordination problems at the top of the ladder; it does not hand over a recipe.

Treat L5 as the direction the ladder points — useful for designing guardrails, routes and monitoring now — rather than a level to announce. The software factory concept's light and dark routes are the same idea from the release side: a dark route describes release without a human reader only where that route is expressly authorised. Evidence alone does not grant release authority; otherwise retain the applicable human decision.

Step back down

Maturity is not a ratchet. The Concepts page already states the regression rule: "If incidents or undone changes become more common, restore human review." Operationally, that means:

  • Stop or pause the route when evidence is missing, monitoring fails or harm increases; restore the applicable human review and use the tested recovery plan. Track the Osmani metrics per task type; a rising intervention rate or defect escape rate is the signal to lower the setting for that task.
  • Keep the run contract current — scope, stopping condition and escalation paths decay as the codebase changes.
  • Remember Fowler's caution about maturity models: the true outcome of an assessment "isn't what level you are but the list of things you need to work on to improve"[7]. A level is a diagnostic, not a badge.
